Glassmorphism

An interface style of the 2020s: semi-transparent panels with a strong background blur, rounded corners, and a thin light edge, placed over vivid gradients or colorful shapes so that the color shows through as a soft glow. The designer Michał Malewicz named it in 2020. Microsoft’s Fluent design system calls the same material Acrylic.

Airy / Layered / Luminous / Premium / Calm

Visual grammar

  • Frosted glass. Panels have a semi-transparent white or tinted fill and a strong background blur. Shapes behind them show as soft, out-of-focus color.
  • Light edge. A 1 px border in translucent white marks the edge of the glass. A soft, wide shadow lifts the panel.
  • Vivid backdrop. Saturated gradients or large colored blobs sit behind the glass, often violet, pink, blue, and orange on a dark or light base. The glass itself stays neutral.
  • Floating cards. Content sits in separate rounded cards that float above the backdrop. Depth comes from layer order and from different levels of opacity, not from perspective.
  • Clean sans-serif. Geometric or neo-grotesque sans-serif type, often white on dark glass or dark on light glass, with little decoration.
  • Large radii. Corners are round, typically 12–24 px on cards and fully rounded on buttons and chips.
  • Abstract color fields. Gradient spheres, mesh gradients, and colorful photos serve as the backdrop. The glass panels themselves carry little or no imagery.

What connects the references

The references confirm the recipe that the record gives. Malewicz’s naming article lists four traits: background blur, floating layers, vivid color, and a subtle light border. Its header image and the Smart Calendar App shot that it cites show all four. The Hype4 generator turns them into CSS: a 15 % white fill, a 20 px blur, a 20 px radius, and a 1 px border at 30 % white.

The style names a material that operating systems already had. iOS 7 brought blurred layers to phones in 2013, Fluent Acrylic fixed a recipe of blur, tint, and noise in 2017, and macOS Big Sur showed it on a vivid wallpaper in 2020. visionOS and Liquid Glass continue it, but over rooms and photos and with refraction. The web version depended on backdrop-filter, which Chrome shipped in 2019.

Real websites in the full style are rare. About 55 candidates were captured and three were kept: Genesis and Mercury Weather as clear examples, and Reflect as borderline. Most product sites use glass only on the navigation bar or show glass as rendered imagery. The css.glass generator passes every metric but was dropped because it describes the style. On real sites the blur sits on a minority of boxes, so the blur threshold was lowered from 0.5 to 0.3.

Two limits of the measurement remain. A photo backdrop keeps the chromatic share low (Genesis: 0.10), so judge photo-backed glass by the rubric. Real glass cards often use gradient fills and inset shadows instead of a CSS border, so Genesis and Reflect fail the border and gradient metrics and also pass the Frutiger Aero fingerprint.

Identity

Name
Name used by designers and vendors
Also called
Glassmorphic, Glasmorphismus, Acrylic (Microsoft Fluent)
Era
2020–present. Named in 2020 and popular in web and app concepts from 2020–2021. Apple’s Liquid Glass (2025) and other operating systems brought translucency back into mainstream interfaces. Fluent Acrylic (2017) is an earlier implementation under another name.
Regions
International
Wikidata
Q138454357
Name used by
Wikipedia: Glassmorphism, Nielsen Norman Group: Glassmorphism: Definition and Best Practices (Megan Brown, 2024-06-07), Michał Malewicz: Glassmorphism in user interfaces (Hype4 Academy; body behind a login, title and author checked), t3n: Design-Trend 2021: Das ist Glasmorphismus (Dieter Petereit, 2021-03-11), Everyday UX: Glassmorphism in 2025 (Jess Eddy, 2025-08-12)

Lineage

  • Descends from Neumorphism. Wikipedia and t3n (2021) describe glassmorphism as the successor of neumorphism. Malewicz, who by his own account started the neumorphism trend a year earlier, named glassmorphism in 2020. It keeps the floating card but replaces low-contrast extruded shadows with translucency and color.
  • Influenced by Fluent Design System (Acrylic). Microsoft’s Fluent Design System (2017) defines Acrylic, a translucent, blurred material. NN/g and t3n both name it as glassmorphism under another name.
  • Influenced by Windows Aero. Wikipedia, citing UXMA, names the glass window borders of Windows Vista and Windows 7 as precursors.
  • Related to Frutiger Aero. Both use translucent glass. Frutiger Aero adds a gloss highlight, reflections, sky gradients, and nature imagery. Glassmorphism uses matte, frosted glass over abstract color.
  • Related to Flat design. Wikipedia reports that glassmorphism began to replace flat design in interface design by the mid-2020s. The content inside the glass stays flat.
  • Related to Liquid Glass. Apple’s 2025 design language. Wikipedia and Everyday UX treat it as a development of glassmorphism that adds refraction, specular edges, and motion.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Panels are translucent, and the shapes behind them look blurred through the panel.
  • A vivid gradient or colorful shapes sit behind the panels.
  • Panels have a thin, light border and rounded corners.
  • Panels float as separate cards with soft shadows.

Rules it out

  • Panels are opaque, or translucent without any blur.
  • A glossy highlight band on the upper half of buttons or panels.
  • Visible material textures such as leather, wood, or brushed metal.
  • Hard offset shadows or thick black outlines.

Often confused with

Frutiger Aero
Frutiger Aero glass is glossy, with a bright highlight on the upper half, reflections, sky-and-water gradients, and nature imagery. Glassmorphism glass is matte and frosted, and the backdrop is abstract color.
Neumorphism
Neumorphism shapes are opaque and the same color as the background. They rise or sink through paired light and dark shadows. Glassmorphism panels are translucent and contrast with a colorful backdrop.
Flat design
Flat design uses opaque, solid fills with no blur and little depth. Glassmorphism keeps the content flat but puts it on translucent, blurred layers over color.
Skeuomorphism
Skeuomorphic interfaces imitate specific physical objects and textures. Glassmorphism uses only one abstract material, frosted glass, and keeps the content flat.
Liquid Glass
Apple’s Liquid Glass bends and magnifies what is behind it and adds moving specular edges. Classic glassmorphism only blurs and tints.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Put a vivid gradient or large colored shapes behind the content, so that the glass has something to blur.
  • Give panels a translucent fill (10–40 % white or a tinted dark), a background blur of 12–40 px, a 1 px translucent white border, and a radius of 16–24 px.
  • Lift panels with a wide, soft shadow of low opacity.
  • Use layers of different opacity to show hierarchy: the more opaque the panel, the more important the content.
  • Use a clean sans-serif and keep the content inside the glass flat.
  • Give the primary action an opaque fill so that it stands out from the glass.

Keep the function

  • Do not put text directly on the busy backdrop. Put it on glass that is opaque and blurred enough for a contrast of at least 4.5:1.
  • Do not use translucency without blur. Clear transparency makes text hard to read.
  • Do not stack many glass layers on top of each other.
  • Do not add gloss highlights, reflections, or material textures.
  • Do not depend on backdrop-filter alone. Give the panel a fill that stays readable when the browser does not support blur or the user asks for reduced transparency.

Useful directions: operating system and app interfaces, dashboards and widgets, fintech and crypto landing pages, music and media players, product launch pages.

Poor fits:

  • Text-heavy interfaces and products where accessibility is critical. Text on translucent panels often fails contrast checks.
  • Low-power devices. Backdrop blur is expensive to render.
  • Dense data tables.
